Hardware Pick-and-Place Flights, 9 and 10 October

T650 aerial manipulator, whole-body 4-D L1 controller, EKF2-fused feedback. Four flights: PP-1 at 17:25, PP-2 at 18:02 and PP-3 at 18:18 on 9 October 2026, from the bag 1009 - T650-AM whole-body Pick&Place, and PP-4 at 19:07 on 10 October, from 1010 - T650-AM whole-body Pick&Place. Times are seconds from the start of each bag. Updated on 12 October with PP-4.

  • 6. Method and data
Overall, after the 10 October flight. The pick works. The place reached the hat for the first time and was lost in the second after the touchdown. The link freeze of 9 October has a known cause and did not come back.
  • Pick, PP-4: hooked and lifted, as in PP-2. The gripper closed 10 mm from its target, with the fingers 4 to 8 mm under the arch.
  • Place, PP-4: the basket touched down on the hat, 85 mm from its centre. 0.4 s later the vehicle began to move back, 23 cm in one second, with the gripper still closed on the stem. It pulled the basket over the rim 0.9 s after the touchdown. The gripper was told to open 1.4 s after the touchdown.
  • Your question 1, the 5 s trim window: it did not help in this flight. Place was pressed 5.0 s after arrival, so the window held the whole arrival swing and the descent was moved 43 mm the wrong way. Without the trim the claw would have come down 24 mm from its target instead of 67 mm (Section 3.2).
  • Your question 2, the offsets: Pick x + 0.01 and EE Offset z = 0.16 worked. EE Offset z is the tightest of them, not a conservative one. Place x − 0.03 went the right way and is about 3 cm too little for the way the basket hung. An EE Offset y of +0.02 is missing (Sections 3.1 and 3.2).
  • Your question 3, what to improve: release the basket at the touchdown, not at the end of the descent. That comes before the platform, the offsets and the payload weight, which all help (Section 5).
  • Link freeze: the MicroXRCEAgent on the Orin had locked itself up under real-time priority. The fix was committed on the Orin 27 minutes before PP-4, which flew 69 s in DIRECT with no gap over 15 ms on the Pixhawk's 400 Hz topics (Section 4.2).
  • End of PP-4: the pilot took STAB at 1.16 m. The motors stopped at 1.42 m, the vehicle fell and came to rest tipped at 36°. It is the third takeover that ended on the floor at an angle (Section 4.1).
85 mmfrom the hat's centre when the basket touched down in PP-4. On 9 October it came down on the rim
23 cmthe vehicle moved back in the second after the touchdown, gripper still closed
1.4 sfrom the touchdown to the command that opens the gripper
43 mmthe 5 s trim moved the descent, away from the target

  • How the 10 October points were read. On the Pick row x has two decimals and y and z have four. On the Place row x and z have two and y has four. The two-decimal numbers were typed and the others came from Get. With what you described, that is Pick = Get x + 0.01 and Place = Get x − 0.03, Get z − 0.01. The pick point is 6 mm ahead of where the basket stood, which fits a Get good to 4 mm plus the 0.01.
  • Where the place hat stood. The Get on the Place row was therefore at (−1.08, −1.104) with the basket's centre at 0.88 m. This page takes that as the centre of the place hat. In the flight the basket lay flat on that hat with its centre at 0.882 m, which agrees, and the video shows it touching down between the hat's centre and its near rim.
  • The pillars had moved since 9 October. The basket rested 10 cm from its 9 October position on the pick hat and 36 mm higher.

2. Whole-body controller overall performance

Accurate without a payload. With this payload it flies stably but not accurately enough to place. Unloaded, the claw hovers within 22 mm rms of its target and the airframe tracks the moving legs to 39 mm rms. With the 190 g basket, which is not in the controller's model, the hover error doubles to 45 mm rms and the lift costs a 25 cm excursion. PP-4 on 10 October confirms this and adds two things: the arm's commands reached its torque caps (Section 4.2), and joint 2 stuck and slipped under the load (Section 4.1).

Settled hover, without and with the payload

The basket doubles the hover error. Without a payload the claw hovers 22 mm rms from its target and stays inside 43 mm for 95 % of the time. With the basket it is 45 mm rms and 84 mm. Both the standing offset and the wander grow. The height holds to a few millimetres in both cases.

RMSE is the root mean square of measured minus reference, so it holds both the standing offset and the wander. The claw's height error with the basket is mostly its 7 mm sag under the load.

What this means for the pick and the place
  • Pick, no payload. The gripper closes when the claw is within 20 mm of its target and within 3 mm across the stem. The unloaded claw is inside 20 mm for 67 % of the time, so the close comes after a wait of a few seconds. All three picks closed 3 to 12 mm from the target. The hover is good enough for the pick.
  • Place, with the basket. The basket is 110 × 115 mm and the hat is 200 mm across. All four corners are on the hat only when the basket's centre is within 20 mm of the hat's centre. Beyond roughly 70 mm the basket tips off. The loaded claw is within 50 mm for 67 % of the time and within 70 mm for 90 %. On top of that the basket hangs 20 to 30 mm away from where the planner assumes (Section 3.2). So the place is the harder half, as you expected, and the loaded hover alone uses most of the hat.
  • Arrival is worse than the settled hover. In the first 2 to 3 s above the place the offset was 36 mm without the basket and 47 mm with it. Both Place commands were given in that time.
  • Height is not the limit. It holds to ±5 mm without and ±6 mm with the basket. The claw sags 7 mm under the load.
  • What the loaded error looks like. The basket's weight acts 0.25 m ahead of the centre of mass, which is 0.45 N·m nose down (Section 4.1), and the attitude error rose from 0.02 rad rms before the lift to 0.06–0.10 rad with the basket. The standing offset was the same in all three loaded hovers: about 25 mm toward world +x and 10 mm toward +y, at headings of 0° and 180°. It is fixed to the room, not to the vehicle. I do not know its cause. An earlier version of this page tied it to the standing attitude error. The sizes match but the signs do not, so that explanation is withdrawn. On 10 October the settled loaded hover above the place sat (−17, −8) mm from its target, the other way, so the offset is not fixed to the room either. It looks like the slow part of the wander.
  • How much data this is. The loaded numbers come from one flight and 23 s of settled hover. Treat them as a first measurement.
PP-4, 10 October
  • Settled, it was better than on 9 October. In the last two seconds above the place the claw was 22 mm rms from its target: an offset of 19 mm and 12 mm of wander, inside 41 mm for 95 % of the time. PP-2's loaded hovers gave 45 mm rms. It is 3 s of data.
  • Arrivals were worse. At the place start the claw was 100 mm rms from its target for three seconds and 186 mm at worst. Above the place it overshot by 87 mm one second after arriving.

3. Pick-and-place precision

On 10 October the targets put the basket on the hat. What lost it was the second after the touchdown, not the typed points. The pick worked on both days with the same EE Offset. The place came down 85 mm from the hat's centre, where on 9 October it came down on the rim. The vehicle then moved back 23 cm with the gripper still closed on the stem. Section 3.1 covers the pick and its offsets. Section 3.2 covers the place: how the basket hangs, the touchdown, the trim window and the place offsets.

The frame is the basket's: x is the direction the claw slides in along, y is along the arch, z is up. The planner columns use the fused odometry and PX4's attitude, which is what the planner and the arm ground station gate on. On 9 October the two columns differed by 4 to 10 mm in height. On 10 October they agree to 1 mm at the pick (Section 4.1).

PP-4, 10 October
  • The rotor wash moved the basket before the grasp. Between 22.2 and 22.6 s, as the vehicle arrived 0.41 m away and 0.25 m higher, the basket slid 21 mm across the hat and turned by 7.5°. In the hover behind the stem it sits under the edge of the front rotor discs. Before that it had shifted by up to 4 mm while the vehicle was still more than a metre away. The pick point had been captured earlier, so it was 18 mm to the side of the basket when the claw slid in.
  • Get and the +0.01 shift did their job. The pick point was (+6.1, −2.5, −0.5) mm from the basket's pose in the first seconds of the bag: Get to 4 mm, plus the 10 mm typed. The claw stopped 10 mm short of its target, as it tends to, and the gripper closed with the fingers 2 mm from the hanger plane.
  • EE Offset z = 0.16 left 4 to 8 mm under the arch. The basket left the hat when the claw reached 171 mm above the basket's centre. During the slide-in the fingers passed 8 mm under that height on average and 4 mm at the least. On the handle the gap was 6 mm.
  • The jaws centre on a point 20 mm to the left of the basket body's origin. This is new. At the close the claw sat 22 mm to the left of the basket's origin, by mocap, and the closing jaws moved the basket by only 1 mm. While the basket hung, its origin stayed 15 to 24 mm to the right of the claw (Section 3.2). On 9 October the claw closed centred on the origin, the jaws pushed the basket 30 mm sideways, and it then hung 11 to 20 mm to the right. Both days agree: the stem is about 20 mm to the left of where obj_0 puts the basket's centre, seen along the approach. On 10 October the push from the rotor wash happened to cancel it.
  • The lift pushed the vehicle forward by 23 cm, with 6.4° of tilt, and joint 2 gave way by 10°. The basket had moved 64 mm forward and 65 mm sideways by the time it was 14 mm up. It left the hat on a slope, as on 9 October.
PP-2 and PP-3, 9 October
  • Get is accurate. The capture differed from the basket's resting pose by (−2.3, −1.9, −0.4) mm in PP-2 and (−2.7, −2.6, −0.6) mm in PP-3, and by 0.03° in yaw.
  • EE Offset x is right. At the close in PP-2 the claw sat 21 mm behind the basket centre in the planner's frame and 27 mm by mocap. The hanger plane is 27.5 mm behind the basket centre in the CAD file.
  • EE Offset z = 0.16 is close to the limit. The basket lifted off when the claw reached 167 mm in the planner's frame, so the fingers passed 7 mm under the arch. While the claw waited on the handle its height ranged from 152 to 167 mm.
  • EE Offset z = 0.20 is above the arch. In PP-3 the claw waited on the handle at (−38 ± 9, −10 ± 6, 194 ± 4) mm in the planner's frame, for a target of (−20, 0, 200), and the gripper closed at (−32, −4, 192) mm. That is 25 mm above the height where the fingers meet the arch, and the basket never moved.
  • The close pushed the basket. In PP-2 the gripper was told to close with the claw within 1 mm of the basket's origin across the stem, and the jaws then moved the basket 30 mm across the hat. An earlier version of this page put that down to the claw drifting during the close. With PP-4 the simpler reading is the 20 mm between the stem and the body's origin.

What limits the pick is the hover, not the setpoint. In PP-1's 39 s wait behind the stem the claw's error had a mean of 4 mm, a standard deviation of 15, 16 and 3 mm in x, y and z, a peak-to-peak of 67, 79 and 14 mm and a period of 6 to 7 s.

Were the pick offsets right?

Yes, and one offset is missing. EE Offset (−0.02, 0, 0.16) picked the basket on both days, and Pick x + 0.01 put the fingers 2 mm from the hanger plane on 10 October. None of them is too conservative in the sense of holding margin you could give back: EE Offset z has the least margin of all. The missing one is EE Offset y.

The stem and the open jaws

Between the start of the slide-in and the close the claw's sideways error reached 30 mm in PP-4, 17 mm in PP-2 and 25 mm in PP-3. The open jaws must clear the stem by more than that on each side, so the open gap less the stem's width should be at least 60 mm. Please measure the new stem against the open gripper.

3.2 Place

How the basket hangs on the claw

The planner assumes the basket sits under the claw at the place as it does at the pick: centre 20 mm ahead of the claw and level. Hanging, it does not. Once lifted, the basket tilts with its top forward and its centre swings back toward the vehicle: 17 mm behind the claw in PP-2 and 27 mm in PP-4, where the planner assumes 20 mm ahead. So even with the claw exactly on its target the basket comes down 37 and 47 mm before the place point. That is what "short" means on this page.
What the planner assumes about the grasped basket
  • It plans the claw, not the basket. It holds two points and one vector. The points are where the basket's centre is at the pick, from Get, and where it should be at the place. Both mean the origin of the mocap body obj_0. The vector is the EE Offset, from that centre to the claw's grasp point.
  • Claw target = point + EE Offset, at both ends. The offset is turned to the yaw of each point. With (−0.02, 0, 0.16) the claw's target is 20 mm behind the centre and 160 mm above it at the pick, and the same at the place.
  • Nothing else. There is no payload in the planner: no mass, no swing, no tilt, and nothing that follows the basket after the grasp. Using one offset at both ends is the assumption that the basket is carried rigidly and level, where it was when the gripper closed, with its centre 20 mm ahead of the claw and 160 mm below it.
  • At the pick that holds by construction, because the basket stands on the hat and the claw is flown to it. The 0.01 typed onto Pick x only moves the claw 10 mm further in. At the place the basket hangs from the arch. In Fig. 5 the dashed outline is the assumption and the coloured outlines are where the basket was.

Where the 47 mm comes from

The basket hangs from the arch, which rests on the fingers. Just before the touchdown:

Along the heading, + is ahead [mm]PP-2PP-4
The arch sits on the fingers this far toward their tips from the grasp point+8+12

  • The tilt is the large part. A level basket hanging from the same arch would have its centre 36 and 40 mm ahead of the claw. The tilt moves it back by 53 and 67 mm.
  • A free hang would be 9°. The hanger is 27.5 mm behind the centre and the arch 167 mm above it, so a basket pivoting freely on its arch tilts by that much and no more. The rest comes from the grip, under the next heading.
  • The tilt grows through the flight: 10, 16 and 18° in PP-2, and 14, 19 and 22° in PP-4. So the offset is not one fixed number. The value just before the touchdown is the one that sets where the basket lands. At the touchdown itself PP-2 read 35 mm.
  • To the side it is the same on both days: the basket's origin is 11 to 24 mm to the right of the claw, and more with the arm yawed in the carry pose. Section 3.1 gives the reason.
  • The tilt changes the touchdown. A basket tilted by 22° meets the hat with its far edge first, about 20 mm before it would lie flat, and has to rotate down while the claw keeps descending.
What sets the angle: the closed gripper holds the stem

A basket pivoting freely on its arch would hang at one angle whatever the claw did. It does not. Fig. 6 puts the basket's tilt beside the pitch of the fingers for the whole time it hangs.

  • Just after the lift it hangs freely. The lift is a jolt and the stem slips in the jaws. The basket settles at 10° in PP-2 and 14° in PP-4, near the free-hang angle, while the fingers point 28 and 29° down.
  • After that it turns with the claw. Changes of the fingers' pitch faster than 2 s appear in the basket's tilt at 64 % in PP-2 and 84 % in PP-4. In PP-4's carry joint 2 jumps by up to 9°, and the basket jumps with it.
  • From the carry to the touchdown the fingers pitch down further, from 12 to 23° in PP-2 and from 9 to 22° in PP-4. The place pose points the claw 10° lower than the carry pose, and the arm gives a few degrees more in the descent. The basket follows 57 and 73 % of that: from 12 to 18° and from 13 to 22°.
  • In simulation the basket only hung freely. Up to 12 October the simulation carried the first handle, with its 3 mm stem, and the simulated claw cannot close below about 19 mm, so it never gripped the stem. In 5 missions recorded on 8 and 9 October the basket hangs at 8 to 10° from the carry to the touchdown, while the fingers' pitch goes from 9 to 21°, and its centre stays within 9 mm of the point under the claw. The simulation had the free-hang part and not the grip part, so it never showed the 37 to 47 mm. Since 13 October the simulation carries this holder, with a 20 mm pad on the fin for the claw to close on. In one flight the clamped basket turned with the claw one to one, where the real stem slips. So it still does not show the hang offset.
  • So the tilt at the touchdown has two parts. About 9° is the free hang, which the handle's shape sets. The other 9 and 13° is the claw turning the gripped basket. Section 5.3 uses this for the handle.
Is it the new handle?
  • The basket hangs back on both days. On 9 October, with the old handle, its centre was already 17 mm behind the claw before the touchdown.
  • On 10 October it reads 10 to 13 mm further back and 4° more tilted, at each of the three stages. A difference that constant comes from something that changed between the two days, not from one flight's swing. The extra 4° at an arch height of 171 mm is 12 mm, so the two readings are one change.
  • Two things changed, and the bag cannot tell them apart. One is the handle. Its arch is 8 mm higher above the basket's origin, 171 against 163 mm at the lift, and a different weight on top changes the angle the basket hangs at. The other is the mocap body. On 10 October it reads 3.3° of tilt while the basket stands on the pick hat, against 0.2° on 9 October, and the 180° flips of 9 October are gone (Section 4.1). So the body was probably defined again in Motive, and its origin and axes may sit slightly differently in the basket. The tilts here have that resting reading taken out, which is right only if the pick hat is level.
  • For the place it does not matter which. Get on the Place row captures the same origin with the basket standing on the hat. What Place x has to carry is how far that origin hangs from where the planner assumes it, 47 mm on 10 October. A ground check with the basket hooked gives that number for any handle and any body (Section 5.2).

The second after the touchdown
  • What moved the vehicle. The hanging basket had been pulling the nose down with 0.6 N·m, and the controller's observer had learned to hold against it. When the hat took the weight, that moment was gone within about 0.3 s, faster than the observer lets go. The airframe pitched 4.2° nose up and moved back at up to 0.32 m/s. The arm sprang up for the same reason.
  • It is the lift in reverse. At the lift the vehicle was pushed 23 cm forward on 10 October and 27 cm on 9 October. PP-2 showed no push at its set-down because the hat never took the basket's weight there.
  • Why the basket came along. Two things held it to the claw. The gripper was still closed on the stem. And the fingers never came clear of the arch: the claw should have gone on down to about 3 cm below the arch contact, but after the touchdown it stayed 21 mm above its planned height, within a few millimetres of the arch (Fig. 9, top). In the middle panel the basket moves with the airframe from 73.3 s on.
  • The simulation. Up to 12 October the simulated claw never gripped the stem, and the simulated vehicle moved back 11 to 15 cm at the set-down. In the flight the pads close fully and the vehicle moved 23 cm. With the holder and the grip pad in the simulation (13 October, one flight) the vehicle moves back 22 cm and drags the clamped basket 6 cm across the hat before the release.
  • How little time there was. From the touchdown: the airframe was moving after 0.36 s, the basket was over the rim after 0.92 s, the leg ended after 1.31 s, the open command came after 1.38 s and the fingers were open after 1.68 s.
  • Why the leg ran on for 1.3 s. The planned bottom was 56 mm below the claw's height at the touchdown, and a planned leg slows to rest at its end, so those last millimetres are its slowest part. Three things add up to that distance: the tilted basket touches about 20 mm early, the claw's target is about 20 mm under the arch contact so that the fingers come free, and the trim lowered it by another 12 mm.
  • A basket set down on the hat's centre would have been pulled off too. It would have had 100 mm to the rim, not 17. The airframe had moved 100 mm by 73.45 s, still 0.5 s before the leg ended.

Did the longer trim window help?

Not in this flight. The window was 5 s and Place was pressed 5.0 s after the claw arrived, so the average covered the whole arrival swing. The descent was moved 43 mm, 38 of them toward the vehicle. Without that shift the claw would have reached the touchdown 24 mm from its typed target. With it, it was 67 mm away.

  • Two thirds of it was the arrival. From 3 s after arrival the same average was (+13, +5) mm. The claw overshot by 87 mm one second after arriving and needed about three seconds to come back.
  • This is what the 9 October replay predicted. For a press at exactly 5 s it gave a trim error of 49 mm (the last part of this section). The flight gave 43 mm of trim, of which about 30 mm was error. The rule that came with the 5 s window was to wait at least 8 s. It was not kept, and nothing in the planner or on the ground station asks for it.
  • Even the settled average did not predict the landing. The settled claw sat 13 mm beyond its target. At the touchdown, 7 s later, it was 22 mm behind its path. The loaded hover wanders by 25 to 30 mm with a period of 5 to 7 s, and with the trim on the bottom of the descent comes 7 s after the press, against 3 s with it off.
  • The trim also moved the bottom down by 12 mm, because the claw read that much high during the wait. That lengthened the slow end of the descent (the place, above).
  • At the pick the window did nothing, and that was fine. Pick was pressed 1.5 s after arrival. Less than half the window had filled, so the planner applied no shift. The claw was 39 mm from its target at the press, and the ground station held the close until it was within 10 mm.
  • Against 9 October. PP-2 pressed after 0.8 s with a 1 s window and got 57 mm. PP-4 pressed after 5.0 s with a 5 s window and got 43 mm. The longer window is not worse, and it cannot help while the press comes inside the arrival. Section 5.5 has what I would change.

The place offset went the right way and needs to go further. Place x − 0.03 covered two thirds of the hang. EE Offset x and y are shared with the pick (Section 3.1), so the place point has to carry what the hang adds.

What a Pick or Place press does

The planner does not wait for the error to converge. It accepts the press as soon as the approach leg has ended, takes the claw's average error over the trim window as "the hover error", and shifts the descent by it. A press during the arrival swing therefore builds that swing into the descent. For the pick the ground station catches it afterwards. For the place nothing does.
At the press: the planner
  1. Refused only in three cases: the approach leg is still flying, the claw's latest error is more than 50 mm away from its own average over the trim window, or that average is larger than 150 mm.
  2. The 50 mm is not a distance to the target. With the descent trim on, which is the default and what flew, the check compares the claw with its own recent average. It measures how fast the claw is moving. A claw 76 mm from its target and drifting slowly passes.
  3. The shift. That average becomes the trim. The planner moves the descent by it so that a claw with a steady offset lands on the target. If the claw sits behind its target, the descent moves forward by the same amount. If the claw is past its target, the descent moves back. A shift over 5 mm is flown sideways first, held 2 s, then the claw goes straight down.
  4. No shift before half a window. If the claw has been above the target for less than half the trim window, the planner applies no shift at all. That is what happened at PP-4's Pick.
After the descent: the ground station
  • Pick. The gripper closes only when the claw is within 20 mm of its target and within 3 mm across the stem. Until then the claw waits on the handle. A hurried Pick costs a few seconds, not the grasp.
  • Place, hook grasp. The gripper opens at the bottom of the descent whatever the error, and Exit To Place starts at once. The Place press is the last decision.

  • Even PP-1's Pick, after a 39 s wait and with the claw 7 mm from its target, got an 18 mm shift. The hover wanders with a 5 to 7 s period, so a one-second average is a sample of the wander, not a steady offset.
The replay on the 9 October hovers: trim off, or trim on and wait longer?

Waiting removes the arrival swing. It does not make a one-second trim right. Replaying the planner's rule on the three long hovers of these flights: if Place or Pick had been pressed at any instant of the hover, the claw would reach the bottom this far from its target (rms / 95 % inside, mm).

SettingPP-2 at the place, basket on the claw, 21 sPP-1 behind the stem, no payload, 39 sPP-3 after the missed pick, no payload, 22 s
Trim off48 / 8522 / 4311 / 20
Trim on, 1 s window, as flown70 / 17334 / 5516 / 29
Trim on, 5 s window38 / 5727 / 469 / 19

With the trim off the claw is at the bottom 3.2 s after the press. With it on, the shift is flown first and held 2 s, and the bottom comes 8.4 s after the press, as in both flown places.

  • The one-second trim is the worst setting in every hover, settled or not. Waiting longer with the window left at one second does not help.
  • Off removes the harm. With the basket it leaves 48 mm rms, because the loaded hover has a steady offset that nothing then removes. In all three loaded hovers of PP-2 the claw sat about 25 mm toward world +x and 10 mm toward +y from its reference, at both headings.
  • A long window removes that offset and leaves the wander, which is 34 mm rms with the basket. The 22 mm in the table comes from only 3 s of possible press times, so read it as "about the wander", not as 22.
  • Without a payload a long window costs nothing: 23 against 22 mm and 7 against 11 mm.
  • Waiting for a small reading before pressing does not help with the trim off. Pressing only when the error reads under 30 mm still lands at 46 mm rms, because the hover moves on during the descent.
The 5 s window, decided on 10 October

pick_place_descent_trim_window_s has been 5 s in the hardware pick-and-place yaml since 10 October, which both hardware controllers' planner reads. The simulation files keep 1 s. The table is the 9 October replay that came with the decision. PP-4 pressed at 5.0 s and its trim was about 30 mm wrong, close to the 49 mm in the second row (the trim window, above).

  • The window only works with the wait. At exactly 5 s the average still holds the first seconds of the arrival, when the loaded claw is 60 to 140 mm off.
  • The decoupled controller reads the same planner block. It relies on the trim for its steady 5 cm offset, so there too the press must come at least 5 s after arrival, or the descent is not trimmed.

4. Problems in the flight test

Open problems first, in order of how much they matter for the next flight. Then the ones that are closed.

4.1 Open problems

The set-down pulls the basket off the hat (PP-4)

Section 3.2. When the hat takes the basket's weight the vehicle moves back 23 cm within a second, and the gripper, still closed on the stem, takes the basket with it. The ground station opens the gripper only when the descent leg has ended, 1.4 s after the touchdown. PP-2 never reached this point, because its basket came down on the rim and the hat never took its weight. Section 5.4 has the fix.

The descent trim moves the place the wrong way (PP-1, PP-2, PP-4)

Section 3.2. Three places, three shifts toward the vehicle: 36, 55 and 38 mm. The 5 s window did not change that, because the press still came inside the arrival. Section 5.5.

Every pilot takeover has ended on the floor at an angle (PP-1, PP-3, PP-4)

  • PP-1. The vehicle came down to 0.35 m in DIRECT through a drone ground-station target. The pilot took STAB at 0.40 m. It dropped at 1.2 m/s from 0.43 m, pitched from 15° to 49° in one second and stayed at 45° nose down. Disarm came 1.5 s after STAB.
  • PP-3. STAB at 0.44 m. The vehicle climbed to 0.56 m, pitched 28° nose up in the air, hit the floor at 1.75 m/s and came to rest at 57° nose up.
  • PP-4. The pilot took STAB at 74.8 s, 0.8 s after the gripper opened, at 1.16 m and while the vehicle was still swinging from the set-down. It climbed to 1.42 m, travelling at 0.6 m/s. At 76.2 s the motors stopped. The vehicle fell, hit the floor at 3.8 m/s at 76.8 s and came to rest 1.0 m from where the pilot took over, tipped by 36°. PX4 reported disarmed at 76.9 s, after the impact.
  • The flight node and the planner after the takeover. In all three flights the flight node went on reporting DIRECT after the pilot had the vehicle. In PP-1 the planner's tilt guard saw 18.4° and flew its abort: gripper open, arm to the release pose. On the floor the arm followed that reference until joint 2 stopped at 32° against a target of 2°, and joints 2 and 3 held 2.7 and 1.4 N·m, their caps, for the 2.4 s until the bag ended. In PP-4 the guard saw 20.5° during the fall and flew the same abort on the floor for 10 s. The arm met nothing this time and its torque stayed under 1.3 N·m.

Section 5.7 has what to change.

Joint 2 sticks and slips under the load (PP-4)

  • Joint 2 moves in jumps. Its reference in the carry pose is 38°. From 46 to 53 s it sat at 36° or at 45° and crossed between them every 2.2 s. The controller's torque command went from 0.6 to 2.3 N·m and back in each cycle. Joint 3 moved between 42° and 47° and the wrist between −2° and 14°.
  • The airframe follows. Its error swung by ±0.15 m at the same period, 193 mm at worst. This is the 100 mm rms of the hover at the place start.
  • The torque is at the caps. The controller commanded up to 2.33 N·m on joint 2, for a cap of 2.44, and 1.32 on joint 3, for a cap of 1.42. With the arm controller's own friction and gravity terms the totals passed the caps and were cut for 0.07 s and 0.10 s, all on the carry leg. They were above 90 % of the caps for 0.5 s and 0.8 s. The whole-body controller is not told when this happens. The caps themselves are in Section 4.2.
  • Servo current while carrying: 197 counts on joint 2 and 115 on joint 3 on average, 378 and 218 at the peaks, over 41 s. On 9 October: 216 and 140, 336 and 204.
  • Joint 2 reached its position guard. The arm controller replaces the commanded torque with its own pull-back above 45°, the real arm's limit. Joint 2 read 45.2° at the top of a jump, and also at 7 to 8 s while holding the home pose, where its reference is 40° and it sits 5° high. It was above 44° for 3.2 s of the flight.
  • Why it sticks. The gearbox friction of these servos grows with the load on the joint. Carrying the basket, joint 2 holds 1.3 N·m, and the torque has to change by about ±0.8 N·m before the joint moves. The controller holds the claw with a soft spring, so the torque builds slowly, the joint breaks loose, overshoots and sticks again.

The rotor wash moves the basket on the pick hat (PP-4)

  • The basket slid 21 mm and turned 7.5° as the vehicle arrived behind the stem (Section 3.1). On 9 October the same arrival moved it by 4 to 6 mm.
  • The pick point is captured before the flight, so the claw then aims at where the basket was. On 10 October the push happened to bring the stem onto the claw's line. A push the other way would have put it 4 cm off.
  • The same wash blows on a basket released at the place while the vehicle backs out. A rim or a rubber mat on both hats would hold it. A lighter basket moves more (Section 5.3).

The basket's mocap body

  • Its origin is not on the stem. The jaws centre about 20 mm to one side of it on both days (Section 3.1). Either EE Offset y carries that, or the body's pivot is moved onto the stem in Motive.
  • Orientation flips. On 9 October the solved orientation jumped by 180° about the vertical whenever the claw was close, and read −179° for five seconds at PP-2's pick. On 10 October it did not flip at the pick. It jumped four times, for single samples, during the turn of the carry. If the markers were moved with the new handle, that worked.
  • Why it matters. The drone's heading at the pick follows the captured yaw. A Get taken during a flip would send the drone to the far side of the pillar and turn EE Offset x around. Since 10 October both Get buttons refuse a yaw that changes by more than 10° inside their half-second window.

PX4's attitude and the mocap attitude disagree in roll

  • On 9 October the two differed by 1.9 to 2.2° in roll and 2.2 to 2.9° in pitch, fixed to the body. On 10 October: 2.5° in roll and 0.2° in pitch before the lift, 1.2° and 0.9° with the basket. The pitch part is gone and the roll part is not.
  • The claw is 0.26 m ahead of the body origin, so pitch is what moves the planner's idea of the claw height. That difference was 4 to 10 mm on 9 October and is 1 mm at the pick and 4 mm at the place on 10 October.
  • EE Offset z is measured in the planner's own frame and already carries whatever is left. It is one more reason not to run it with 4 mm of margin (Section 3.1).

The vertical load: why the controller reads more than 190 g (PP-2, PP-4)

The basket is 190 g. The 0.31 kg in the first version of this report was my conversion, and it was wrong. I divided the step in the controller's thrust command by g. That command is in the controller's own thrust units, which were 7 % larger than delivered newtons at the pick and 13 % larger at the end of the flight, and the step also held battery sag. The pitch moment the basket put on the vehicle corresponds to 1.7 to 1.9 N at the claw, which is 175 to 195 g.

The controller holds no payload mass. Its observer estimates one vertical force: the gap between the thrust it commands and the weight of the vehicle in its model. Everything that changes the thrust command needed to hover lands in that one number. After the grasp that is the basket's weight and four other things.

Without a payload
  • Over the three flights the thrust command for the same hover ranged from 34.3 to 40.3 N as the battery went from 24.2 to 23.0 V. The observer's vertical estimate went from +2.2 to −2.7 N with nothing on the claw.
  • Delivered thrust stayed at 34.5 ± 0.3 N and battery power at 465 ± 5 W in all three flights. These two do not depend on the controller's units, so they are the gauges used below.
  • The delivered-thrust level, 34.5 N, is 6 % under the 36.7 N weight in the controller's model. The calibration was made on the bare airframe, and this vehicle's mass has not been confirmed on a scale. Only changes of the gauge are used here.

Smaller items

  • The controller's own torque limit, wb_tau_max, is 3.0 N·m for every joint, above all four arm caps. When the arm controller cuts a command the whole-body controller is not told. On 10 October that happened for a tenth of a second.
  • DIRECT entry in PP-4 left the airframe 119 mm and the yaw 4.8° from their references for the first four seconds.
  • Battery in PP-4: 23.9 V and 19 A at DIRECT entry, 23.4 V and 22 A with the basket. On 9 October the thrust command for the same hover rose by 2.8 N over PP-1's 150 s as the battery fell (the vertical load, above).
  • The topics recorded from the Orin show no gap over 25 ms in PP-4. On 9 October there was one of 74 to 105 ms, in PP-2.

4.2 Solved problems

The Pixhawk data link froze in hover (PP-2)

The cause was found on the Orin on 10 October and the fix was committed 27 minutes before PP-4. PP-4 flew with a clean link.
Time [s]Evidence
144.67The Pixhawk's 400 Hz sensor and attitude topics and its 100 Hz odometry stop within the same millisecond, and none of its slower topics publishes again. This was 18:04:53. Mocap and every node on the Orin keep running.
144.67–145.67The flight node keeps computing on frozen feedback. Its attitude and position errors do not change for a full second.
145.60Roll 11.6°, yaw −14°, speed 0.62 m/s.
145.67The node logs POSITION FEEDBACK LOST after its 1.0 s gate, reverts to SAFETY and prints "NO feedback of any kind … TAKE MANUAL CONTROL".
145.8–146.0Roll goes from 14.8° back to 1.5°. Speed 1.45 m/s. The vehicle then coasts level.
146.7–147.35Descent at 1.2 to 1.3 m/s and touchdown at (−2.41, −1.51), still moving at 1.1 m/s.
148.2At rest at (−2.70, −2.00), upright, 2.6 m from the hover point and 0.45 m beyond the edge of the 4.5 × 4.2 m field the mission is laid out in.
149.90One sample of each Pixhawk topic arrives, then nothing until the bag ends at 166 s. It is fresh, so the Pixhawk never rebooted. It shows STAB, disarmed by the RC switch, and EKF2 no longer fusing mocap, so the Orin's data was not reaching the Pixhawk either.
  • What it was. The MicroXRCEAgent is the process on the Orin that carries every topic between the Pixhawk and ROS, in both directions. All of its roughly 30 threads ran at real-time priority on one isolated core, with real-time throttling off. When PX4 re-established its session, the Agent's single processing thread had to wait for a reader thread to stop, and that reader was spinning at 100 %. At the same real-time priority on the same core the spinning thread never gave way, so the waiting thread never ran again. Nothing from the Pixhawk reached ROS and nothing from ROS reached the Pixhawk. Backtraces of both threads on the Orin confirmed it. On 10 October the same lock-up lasted more than 20 minutes on the ground, with the ground station showing the Agent's core at 100 %.
  • How that fits PP-2. Every Pixhawk topic stopped within the same millisecond, EKF2 lost its mocap at the same time, the Pixhawk itself kept running, and one stray sample came through five seconds later. PP-3's stream stopping 7 s after disarm has the same signature. The 9 October bags cannot show the session being re-established, so this is the same symptom with a mechanism that was caught in the act a day later.
  • The fix. The Agent keeps its isolated core and runs at ordinary priority (fsc_autopilot_ros2 71ec97a, 10 October 18:40). Under the ordinary scheduler the same spin lasts microseconds.
  • PP-4. In 69 s of DIRECT the Pixhawk's attitude and sensor topics arrived at 400.0 Hz with a largest gap of 15 ms, its odometry at 100.0 Hz with 21 ms, and the control loop ran at 250.0 Hz with 15 ms. It is one flight. Section 5.7 keeps two precautions.

PP-3 missed the pick

EE Offset z had been raised from 0.16 to 0.20 after PP-2, which put the claw above the arch. PP-4 flew 0.16 again and picked the basket. Section 3.1 shows why it should not go above 0.16.

The basket's stream was dead in PP-1

On 9 October /vrpn_mocap/obj_0/pose carried no message for the 192 s of PP-1, while the processor republished one frozen pose at 60 Hz, 11 423 identical samples, with mocap_status reading normal. A Get in that state stores a stale pose. Since 10 October both Get buttons refuse a pose that does not change at all and say why on the status line. In PP-4 the stream was live for the whole flight, at 120 Hz with a largest gap of 35 ms.

The place point was typed without a measurement

On 9 October the place point was typed by hand, and the three flights used three points up to 6 cm apart. The arm ground station now has a Get on the Place row and editable boxes on the Pick row. PP-4 used both, which is why the place hat's position is known in that flight.

Arm torque and the torque caps (PP-2, PP-4)

Raise joint 3's cap by 20 %. Leave joint 2. No command was clipped on 9 October, but joints 2 and 3 came within 3 % of their caps for a few hundredths of a second. On 10 October, with the caps unchanged, both were cut for a tenth of a second (Section 4.1). Joint 3 has room in the servo. Joint 2's limit is heat, which a higher cap does not help.

Applied torque is the servo's measured current times its torque constant. Both peaks came while the arm moved to the carry pose with the basket on it. Without a payload neither joint's applied torque passed 48 % of its cap.

JointCap nowRecommendedWhy
3192 counts, 1.42 N·m230 counts, 1.70 N·mIt has the least headroom, and its cap allows only 25 % of the stall current, against 44 % on joint 2. At 230 counts it is 0.69 A, 30 %. Raise its servo PWM Limit from 330 to 380 in the same change, by the arm repository's own sizing rule. Otherwise the firmware cuts the back-EMF compensation earlier.
2365 counts, 2.44 N·munchangedIts peaks above 80 % lasted 0.36 s in total, and its cap is already 1.0 A. Its real limit is heat. It carried the basket at 180 to 224 current counts for 70 s. The arm repository records an overload shutdown of this joint's servo near 250 counts sustained, on 26 August with a 343 g load. A servo that shuts down in flight leaves the arm limp. A higher cap does not change the sustained current.
1 and 457.6 counts, 0.34 and 0.39 N·munchangedPeaks 0.25 and 0.26 N·m. The basket turned the wrist by 52° because the controller's heading stiffness is soft: it never commanded more than 0.11 N·m on joint 4.
  • A cap protects the servo and whatever the arm pushes against. After PP-1's touchdown the arm pushed into the floor at exactly these caps for 2.4 s (Section 4.1). With joint 3 at 230 counts it would push 20 % harder there. That is the cost of the raise.
  • For joint 2, reduce the heat instead. Keep the loaded part of a flight short, leave two minutes between loaded flights as the arm repository's rule says, and record the servos' temperature. The temperature is read by the arm's hardware interface but is not in these bags.
  • If you still want more on joint 2, 400 counts (2.67 N·m, +10 %) with its PWM Limit at 550 is the most I would add, and only with the temperature recorded.
  • The controller's own limit does not match. wb_tau_max is 3.0 N·m for every joint, above all four arm caps. If the arm ever clips, the controller is not told. It did not happen here. Per-joint limits equal to the arm's caps would close this, and that needs a code change.

5. Further Improvement

Your three ideas first, each with what the two days of data say about it. Then what I would add, and one list in order for the next flight.

5.1 A larger place platform

Yes, and extending it away from the vehicle is the right direction, as long as the place point moves with it. What the basket needs is distance between the point it is aimed at and the rim on the vehicle's side. A larger platform alone would not have completed PP-4.
  • Where the basket has gone so far. In PP-4 it touched down 76 mm short of the hat's centre and 37 mm to the side, and was then pulled 12 cm further toward the vehicle. In PP-2 it came down short again, on the rim. Every miss so far is on the vehicle's side.
  • So the room is needed between the aim point and the near rim. Extending the platform toward world −x and typing the place point further in gives that, without bringing the platform closer to the landing gear. Extending it and leaving the place point where it is adds room on the side the basket has not gone to.
PlatformAim point from the near rim [mm]Basket's centre may land short / long by, before it is over the rim [mm]Short / long by, with all four corners on [mm]
Today: disc, 200 mm across, aimed at its centre100100 / 10020 / 20
200 mm wide, 300 mm deep180180 / 120125 / 65
200 mm wide, 400 mm deep250250 / 150195 / 95
  • What it has to cover. The basket landed 106 mm short of its aim in PP-4 and 164 mm in PP-2. Of that, the trim and the hang can be taken out (Sections 5.2 and 5.5). What remains is the tracking error, 22 and 74 mm in the two flights, and the loaded hover, which stayed within 41 mm for 95 % of the time on 10 October and within 84 mm on 9 October. 300 mm deep covers that. 400 mm would have held PP-2's basket with nothing else changed.
  • Width and the landing gear. The skids are 284 mm apart on the inside and reach 163 mm ahead of the body origin. The basket lands only 66 mm ahead of their tips. At PP-4's touchdown the tips were 41 mm short of the near rim and the skid bottoms 83 mm above the hat's top. At the planned bottom of the descent they would have been about 30 mm above it. Keep the platform no wider than 200 mm so that it passes between the skids. Once the aim point is more than about 7 cm from the near rim the skid tips are alongside its near end, with 42 mm to spare on each side when the vehicle is centred. In PP-4 it was 23 mm off the centre line.
  • Flying higher. In the place pose the skid bottoms are 141 mm below the claw, and the claw has to end below the arch, which is 203 mm above the platform. That puts the skids 30 to 40 mm above the platform at the bottom, whatever its size. A place pose that reaches lower raises the vehicle: [0, 25, 45, 0] by 10 mm and [0, 20, 50, 0] by 16 mm with the claw at the same 20° pitch, the second with joint 3 on its limit. A 60° fold such as [0, 20, 40, 0] gives 46 mm but tilts the claw to 30°, and the hook then needs more friction to keep the arch on the fingers. With this hook there are one to two centimetres to gain.
  • What a larger platform does not do. In PP-4 the claw pulled the basket 12 cm to the rim and the vehicle moved 23 cm. On a larger platform that is a 20 cm drag across it, not a place. The release has to come first (Section 5.4).
  • Give it a rim or a mat. A shallow rim or a rubber mat keeps a released basket in place while the rotors are still above it.

  • The reasons are in Sections 3.1 and 3.2. In short: the basket hangs 47 mm short of where the planner assumes and about 20 mm to the right of the claw, and the fingers passed only 4 mm under the arch.
  • Check the hang on the ground first. These numbers belong to this handle and to this mocap body (Section 3.2). Hook the basket, put the arm in the place pose and compare the basket's position with the claw's. Expect the basket's centre about 27 mm behind the claw and 20 mm to its right. The x to subtract from Get is 20 mm plus the distance behind, plus 10 mm.
  • EE Offset y depends on the mocap body. If the basket's body is defined again in Motive, check it again. If its pivot is put on the stem, EE Offset y goes back to 0.
  • With a larger platform do the Get with the basket standing where you want it to land, and subtract the same 0.06.

5.3 The payload: lighter, and a handle that hangs level

It helps with everything the basket disturbs, in proportion. First weigh the basket: the gauges say it got heavier with the new handle.
  • What scales with the weight. The push at the lift, 23 and 27 cm, and at the set-down, 23 cm. The tilt at both. The loaded hover error. The arm torque. The first three come from one number, the basket's weight times the 0.25 m between the claw and the centre of mass: 0.45 N·m on 9 October and 0.6 N·m on 10 October by the moment gauge. Half the weight is about half the push, 11 to 13 cm.
  • The arm gains the most. Carrying the basket, joint 2 holds 1.3 N·m, of which 0.7 is the basket. Its friction grows with that load, which is what makes it stick and slip, and its peaks reach the cap. At half the weight it holds 0.9 N·m.
  • Weigh it. The load gauges read 0.3 to 0.7 N more than on 9 October (Section 4.1). If the new handle added 30 to 60 g, the first saving is in the handle.
  • What gets worse. The rotor wash. It moved this basket 21 mm and turned it 7.5° on the pick hat before the grasp, and it blows on the released basket at the place while the vehicle backs out. A lighter basket moves more. Give both hats a rim or a mat, and keep the basket's walls open.
  • The other way to the same effect is to tell the controller about the basket (Section 5.6). The weight then still loads the arm, but most of the push at the lift and at the set-down goes.

A handle that hangs level

Tilting the handle is the right kind of change. Lean it forward, away from the vehicle, until the arch is above the basket's centre of mass. Leaning it back toward the vehicle makes the tilt and the offset larger.
  • The basket settles with its centre of mass under the arch. That is where it goes after every jolt (Section 3.2). Standing on the hat, its centre is 27.5 mm ahead of the arch. Hanging, it is under the arch or behind it. Only the handle's shape can remove that difference.
  • Leaning the handle back moves the arch, not the basket. The arch ends up further behind the centre of mass, the basket swings until its centre of mass is under the arch again, and it hangs steeper. To hang level it would need the jaws to hold the basket's 1.9 N at a 62 mm lever. They let go at 27.5 mm in the first second after both lifts.
HandleArch behind the basket's centre [mm]Hangs freely atTilt at the touchdown, PP-2 and PP-4Basket short of the place point with the claw on target [mm]
As flown, stem upright27.59°18 and 22°, measured37 and 47, measured
Stem leaning back 15°, toward the vehicle6221°30 and 34°73 and 82
Stem leaning forward 12°, arch above the centre00°9 and 13°9 and 18

The last two rows are estimates. They assume the basket behaves as in these two flights: it settles at its free-hang angle, the claw then turns it by 9 and 13° more, and the arch sits on the fingers where it did. Same stem length and the same foot as now.

  • With the arch above the centre of mass the basket hangs as it stands. EE Offset x moves forward with the arch, by 27.5 mm to about +0.01, and then describes the pick and the place alike.
  • What is left, 9 to 18 mm and 9 to 13°, is the claw turning the gripped basket between the carry and the touchdown. It goes if the fingers have the same pitch in the carry pose and the place pose, or if the jaws do not grip the stem (Section 5.4).
  • Bench check. Hang the basket by its arch on a round rod. With the arch above the centre of mass it hangs level. The present handle hangs at 9°.

5.4 Release the basket at the touchdown

This is the change that would have completed PP-4. The basket was on the hat. It needed the fingers off the stem within about 0.4 s of the touchdown, and they came off after 1.7 s.
  1. Open on the touchdown, not at the end of the leg. The touchdown shows in the basket's mocap height within a tenth of a second: the basket stops going down while the claw's path continues. The planner already reads obj_0. It can report the touchdown, the ground station opens on that report, and Exit To Place follows as it does now. Two slower signs of the same event are joints 2 and 3 moving by 6° within 0.3 s and the observer's vertical estimate dropping by 1 N within 0.3 s. This is a change in the planner and in the arm ground station. It is not made yet.
  2. Do not grip the stem. The hook does not need a grip. The basket hangs from the arch on the fingers, and the stem between them only keeps it from sliding sideways. With the jaws closed to a gap a few millimetres wider than the stem, the fingers can slide out from under the arch when the vehicle moves back, which is the way Exit To Place backs out anyway, and at the pick the closing jaws no longer push the basket. The ground station has only open and closed today. It needs a third position, or the fingers need a mechanical stop. Check it on the ground first: with the basket standing and the fingers under the arch, pull the claw straight back by hand and see whether the basket stays.
  3. End the descent sooner after the touchdown. No trim in z, and Place z no lower than needed (Section 3.2). In PP-4 that takes the planned distance after the touchdown from 56 to 45 mm. It helps a little and cannot replace the first two.
  4. Centre the touchdown (Section 5.2). It turns 17 mm to the rim into 100 mm, which was 0.8 s in PP-4.
  5. Take the push away (Sections 5.3 and 5.6).

In PP-4 the first of these would have left the basket where it touched down, 85 mm from the hat's centre with its near edge about 4 cm over the rim. With the fourth as well it stands on the hat with all four corners.

5.5 The descent trim

  • For flights with this controller, turn it off: pick_place_descent_trim: false. The planner accepts the change while it runs. Its 50 mm check then compares the claw with the target itself, and the bottom of the descent comes 3 s after the press, not 7 s. In PP-4 the claw would have been 24 mm from its target. This controller has no steady offset for the trim to remove: its settled loaded hover sat (−17, −8) mm from the target on 10 October and (+25, +10) mm on 9 October.
  • The decoupled controller needs the trim for its steady 5 cm offset, and it reads the same planner block. Turn the trim back on for it.
  • If the trim stays on, make the planner wait. Start the average 3 s after the leg has ended, and refuse the press until the window is full, with a status line that counts down. That turns the "wait 8 s" rule into something the planner enforces. It is a small planner change and is not made yet.
  • Leave z out of the trim. The height holds to a few millimetres, and a lower bottom only delays the release.

5.6 The controller and the arm

  • Tell the controller about the basket. Add the basket's mass at the claw to the controller's model while it is hooked, switched by the same events that close and open the gripper. The lift and the set-down are then steps the model expects, and the observer no longer has to learn 0.6 N·m and forget it again. It needs the weighed mass and the hang offsets of Section 3.2, and it is a code change in the flight node. The simulation shows the same push at the set-down, 11 to 15 cm, so it can be developed there first.
  • Joint 3's torque cap is still 192 duty counts. The 9 October recommendation stands: 230 counts, with its servo PWM Limit from 330 to 380 (Section 4.2). On 10 October its command was cut for 0.10 s.
  • Joint 2's cap was reached for 0.07 s. Its limit is heat: it carried 197 current counts on average for 41 s, against the 250 of the August overload shutdown. A lighter basket is the cure here, not a higher cap.
  • Joint 2's position guard. The carry pose asks for 38° and the home pose for 40°, 5 to 7° under the 45° guard, and the joint reached the guard in both. A carry pose with joint 2 at 33°, for example [12, 33, 42, 0], leaves 12°. It opens the fold by 5°, so check the landing gear against the basket in simulation first.
  • Joint 2 sticking and slipping. The 8 October offline study of the arm's friction compensation has two candidate changes for this, neither flown. They are worth a ground test with the basket hooked, where the same jumps should show without flying.

5.7 Takeover, landing and the link

  1. Land as the workflow says: back to SAFETY, then land and disarm from the drone ground station. Revert at 0.8 m or higher, since earlier flights measured a dip of about 20 cm at every revert on this vehicle.
  2. If the pilot takes over in STAB, do it from a steady hover with the throttle stick at hover, and bring the vehicle down under power. In PP-4 the motors stopped at 1.42 m.
  3. Make the flight node report SAFETY as soon as PX4 leaves OFFBOARD or disarms, and make the planner's guard do nothing when the vehicle is not in OFFBOARD. Three flights now show the planner or the arm acting after the pilot had the vehicle. Neither change is made yet.
  4. Watch the MicroXRCEAgent's core on the Orin over the next flights. One clean flight is not a proof.
  5. Shorten the blind second in case the link ever stops again: PX4's COM_OF_LOSS_T at 0.2 to 0.3 s for direct-actuation flights, and a short timeout on attitude and rate in the flight node, which today wait behind the 1.0 s odometry gate.

5.8 In order, for the next flight

  1. Weigh the basket with the new handle.
  2. Handle, if it is printed again: stem leaning forward so the arch is above the basket's centre of mass, and EE Offset x moved forward by the same distance (Section 5.3).
  3. Ground check with the basket hooked and the arm in the place pose: where the basket's centre sits against the claw, and the stem against the open and the closed jaws.
  4. Settings: EE Offset (−0.02, +0.02, 0.15). Pick = Get x + 0.01. Place = Get x − 0.06, Get y, Get z, yaw −180. Margins 0.20 / 0.10.
  5. Descent trim off for the whole-body flight.
  6. Release at the touchdown: the planner and ground-station change of Section 5.4, or jaws that do not grip the stem. Without one of them, a basket that reaches the platform will be pulled off it again.
  7. Place platform: 200 mm wide and 300 mm deep, extended away from the vehicle, with a rim or a mat. Do the Get with the basket standing 18 cm in from the near rim.
  8. Joint 3's cap to 230 counts with its PWM Limit at 380.
  9. First flight back over open floor with the platform on a low stand, and land through SAFETY from 0.8 m.

6. Method and data

  • Bags. flight_wb_l1_4d_pick_and_place_20261009_172557, _180228, _181817 and flight_wb_l1_4d_pick_and_place_20261010_190719, recorded on the ground-station computer.
  • Measured states. Airframe from the fused odometry the controller flies on, and separately from the vehicle's mocap body. Claw by the planner's kinematic model on either pose with the measured joints. The model reproduces the planner's own claw estimate to 0.05 mm.
  • References. The planner's whole-body reference stream.
  • Basket. Its mocap body. On 9 October the basket's resting pose before the approach is the frame at the pick, because the solved orientation flips when the claw is near. On 10 October the frame is the basket's pose in the hover behind the stem, after the rotor wash had moved it, with the approach direction from the captured pick yaw.
  • The place hat on 10 October. Its centre is taken as the typed place point less the 0.03 typed onto Get x. Its top is 32.5 mm under the basket's centre height while the basket lay flat on it, 0.882 m. The basket's footprint and the hat's radius are from the CAD files.
  • Touchdown and the arch. The touchdown is the first sample at which the basket stops descending. The height at which the fingers meet the arch is the claw's height above the basket's centre when the basket has risen 3 mm at the pick: 171 mm by mocap in PP-4, 163 mm in PP-2.
  • Video. VID_20261010_190704.mp4, 20 frames per second. It runs 14.0 ± 0.05 s ahead of the bag: the basket goes over the rim at 87.6 s in the video and 73.6 s in the bag.
  • Scoring windows. DIRECT entry to the controller's last tick with live feedback: 28.0–187.2 s, 14.6–144.6 s, 12.4–80.7 s and 5.8–74.8 s.
  • Hover windows. Spans in which the planner's centre-of-mass and claw references both move slower than 5 mm/s for at least 1.5 s. Settled means without the first 3 s. With the basket: PP-2 from the lift-off at 47.0 s to its removal at 118.3 s, leaving out 89.5–96.5 s when it rested on the hat's rim, and PP-4 from 31.5 s to the touchdown.
  • Load gauges. Delivered thrust is the sum of the squared rotor speeds the motor commands ask for, times a thrust constant that follows the battery voltage and the throttle as fitted on the seven stepped-payload hovers of 20 August. Battery power is voltage times current from PX4's battery status. The moment gauge is the controller's rotational disturbance estimate about the pitch axis, converted with the same thrust ratio.
  • Applied arm torque. The servos' measured current divided by the calibrated counts per newton-metre. The arm's own weight is taken out with the arm controller's calibrated gravity model. A command counts as cut when the streamed torque plus the arm controller's friction and gravity terms, in duty counts, reaches the cap.
  • Not in the bag. The gripper's commands, the PX4 log, the Orin's system log and the pilot's sticks.
  • Files. Tools, numbers and this page's source are in docs/docs_aerial_manipulator/archive/wb_pick_place_flight_20261009/. The 10 October analysis is in wb_pick_place_flight_20261010/ beside it.
